evidence_quotes.quote: The study was conducted in three informal settlements of Dar es Salaam—Goba-Chaurembo, Goba-Kibululu, and Goba-Kunguru—located in the Goba ward of the Ubungo municipality (Fig. 1).
Interviews were conducted with the Ubungo municipal water engineer and two Mtaa (ward leaders), the ward health officer and non-state water service providers, through face-to-face conversation.
The data were then collected from thirty-five (35) non-water service providers through face-to-face interviews using open-ended questions.

According to the Ubungo municipal water engineer, the following formal procedures are required before engaging in the water supply: Firstly, residents are required to register with the municipal council before water supply; secondly, obtain permission from DAWASA; and thirdly, obtain operation permit from the Ministry of Health (MoH). Unfortunately, only the public tanker trucks were registered. However, the municipal water engineer described the actions of the non-registered operators as a “survival strategy” but not as “criminal or illegal act.”

The system of monthly billing (when extended via PVC pipes to residents) could not permit access by all residents, due to the inability of low-income residents to finance the cost of networked water extension.

The conditional rule of cash and carry system governed water access towards the maintenance of the water infrastructure. While clients were allowed to fetch water on credit on the occasion of lack of cash at hand grounded in social relations (as neighbours or relatives), continuous default in payment of water service charges was liable for refusal or denial of water services by the concerned actor (Cain 2018).

criterion_notes.c1: Examines community and household water service provision, infrastructure sustainability, and access in three informal settlements (Goba-Chaurembo, Goba-Kibululu, and Goba-Kunguru) on the periphery of Dar es Salaam underserved by DAWASA.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study directly examines formal and informal water infrastructure governance and state-non-state institutional relations. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although part of the paper describes entrepreneurial resource mobilization and physical infrastructure construction, dedicated empirical sections explicitly analyze rule-type mechanisms directly governing water access: (1) formal municipal council registration, DAWASA permission, and Ministry of Health operating permit requirements alongside street-level regulatory discretion/forbearance ('turning a blind eye' and treating unregistered providers as a survival strategy rather than an illegal act) and DAWASA tanker registration partnerships; (2) tariff and cost-recovery rules, including upfront PVC network connection charges, metered monthly billing, and the 'cash and carry' payment rule; and (3) point-of-access accommodation, eligibility/rationing, and enforcement rules, including credit accommodation for neighbours/relatives, queue priority exemptions for elders, disabled persons, and mothers with infants, domestic-use rationing during scarcity, and denial of water service for continuous payment default.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative empirical case study based on primary fieldwork (June-July 2017 and follow-up in February 2019), comprising motorbike transect reconnaissance, snowball identification of providers to saturation, and face-to-face open-ended interviews with 35 non-state water service providers, the Ubungo municipal water engineer, two Mtaa (ward) leaders, and the ward health officer, coded in MAXQDA. Per review safeguards, qualitative socio-legal/governance studies are eligible for the mechanism synthesis without quantitative effect estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative outcomes relevant to settlement-level water service availability and continuity, high seasonal cost/unreliability of tanker supply, affordability-driven exclusion of low-income households from piped PVC connections under extension-cost and monthly metered billing rules, and access accommodation (credit) versus denial/refusal of water service upon continuous payment default (notwithstanding the authors' note in the conclusion calling for future household-level studies on water access).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (non-state water service providers and municipal/ward officials across three informal settlements in Ubungo municipality, Dar es Salaam), rule-type governance exposures, qualitative access/exclusion/availability outcomes, and qualitative case-study design are clearly identifiable.

study_design: Qualitative case study using motorbike transect reconnaissance, snowball sampling, and open-ended face-to-face interviews coded thematically in MAXQDA
population_and_sample: Three informal settlements in Goba ward, Ubungo municipality, Dar es Salaam, Tanzania (Goba-Kibululu, Goba-Kunguru, and Goba-Chaurembo; total population 16,491 in 3,965 households); primary qualitative sample of 35 non-state water service providers (4 mechanized borehole distributors, 17 water kiosk operators, 1 well operator, 10 tap/standpipe operators, alongside tanker and pushcart operators) plus the Ubungo municipal water engineer, two Mtaa (ward) leaders, and the ward health officer (unit of analysis: non-state water providers and settlement-level water governance).
exposure: Formal and informal regulatory and operational rules governing informal-settlement water supply and access: three-step licensing/registration requirements (municipal council registration, DAWASA permission, Ministry of Health operating permit), municipal regulatory forbearance toward unregistered operators, DAWASA tanker registration partnerships, tariff and cost-recovery rules (upfront PVC connection costs, metered monthly billing, cash-and-carry payment rule), social-relational credit accommodation, payment-default service denial, and kiosk queue-priority and domestic-use rationing rules.
outcome: Continued community water service availability across dry and rainy seasons, exclusion of low-income residents from piped PVC network connections due to upfront extension costs and monthly billing, high dry-season tanker water costs, and temporary water access on credit versus denial/refusal of service for continuous payment default.
rationale: This qualitative empirical study investigates how non-state water providers and state/municipal actors govern water supply and access in three informal settlements of Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. It satisfies all review inclusion criteria under both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope: beyond describing entrepreneurial infrastructure construction, it empirically examines formal registration/permitting rules and municipal regulatory forbearance ('turning a blind eye' to unregistered operators), DAWASA tanker registration arrangements, tariff and cost-recovery rules (PVC connection charges, metered monthly billing, cash-and-carry payment), credit accommodation, queue exemptions, scarcity rationing, and denial of service for continuous payment default, reporting qualitative evidence on service availability, connection exclusion of low-income residents, and payment-related denial of access. Confidence is medium because primary data collection focused on providers and local officials rather than a household sample, as the authors note when calling for further household-level research.
